analysis.one_liner: Bans grocery price gouging and surveillance-based pricing and outlaws electronic shelf labels in large stores.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 11 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar grocery stores from charging 'grossly excessive prices' — prices the Federal Trade Commission could define as 120% or more of the item's average price over the prior six months — unless the store can show the increase came from costs outside its control. It would also ban 'surveillance-based price setting,' meaning charging one shopper a different price than another based on personal data, facial recognition, or electronic shelf tags, and would require large stores to post paper shelf labels instead of digital ones. The FTC, state attorneys general, and individual shoppers could all enforce the rules, with shoppers able to sue for at least $3,000 per violation and courts required to refuse pre-dispute arbitration agreements for these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Grocery shoppers, who would get a federal backstop against sudden unexplained price spikes and against stores charging them personalized prices based on their data, purchase history, or face. Shoppers who are overcharged could recover at least $3,000 per violation in court, without facing mandatory arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits retail food stores from selling items at 'grossly excessive prices,' with an affirmative defense only for cost increases outside the store's control, and directs the FTC to consider defining a grossly excessive price as 120% or more of the item's average price over the prior six months.

Bans surveillance-based price setting, including adjusting a price for a consumer based on personal information collected through facial recognition or electronic shelf labels, while still allowing disclosed, uniform discounts (senior, military, student, loyalty) that apply equally to everyone who qualifies.

Gives shoppers a private right of action with a minimum $3,000 award per violation, triple damages for willful violations, attorney's fees, and a rule that pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers are unenforceable for these claims — and lets state attorneys general sue on residents' behalf.
Requires any store using facial recognition technology to post clear signage at the entrance saying so, and requires stronger state consumer-protection laws to remain in effect.

analysis.who_pays: Large grocery chains, which would face new liability for pricing decisions, lose the ability to use electronic shelf labels and personalized pricing, and bear compliance costs; also the vendors that sell electronic shelf labels and facial-recognition or in-store analytics systems to grocers. Some costs could be passed to shoppers through higher baseline prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large grocery chains and retail tech vendors

drawbacks.text: A price ceiling pegged to the trailing six-month average can block the price signals that ration scarce goods during a supply shock; the bill's affirmative defense for costs 'not within the control' of the store softens but does not eliminate that risk, and enforcement would depend on FTC guidelines that do not yet exist.

The ban on electronic shelf labels applies to the technology itself in stores over 10,000 square feet, even when the tags simply display one honest price for everyone — imposing retrofit costs on large grocers rather than targeting only personalized pricing, which Section 3 already bans.
Leaving 'grossly excessive price' and 'market' to future FTC rulemaking creates legal uncertainty for stores and could produce inconsistent enforcement and litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real: a federal gouging backstop, a ban on charging people different prices based on their data, and a genuine right to sue without arbitration. The main costs fall on large grocery chains and their tech vendors, though some compliance cost could reach shoppers. The blanket electronic-shelf-label ban is the weakest part — it outlaws a useful technology rather than just its abusive use — and the definition of 'grossly excessive' depends heavily on how the FTC writes its rules. On balance the bill is aimed squarely at protecting shoppers, with the sharpest design questions in the price-cap definition and the technology ban.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in February 2026 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has not taken it up; with the session running into January 2027, it could still move, but so far nothing has happened.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Ray Luján introduced the bill on February 12, 2026, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Merkley, Rosen, Gillibrand, and Heinrich.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction; no further action appears in the record.
It has 11 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, and no Republicans.

The bill would be enforced by the FTC as an unfair or deceptive practice, by state attorneys general, and by consumers in court, with pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers ruled unenforceable for these claims.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large grocery chains and retail tech vendors benefit so far, because no new limits on their pricing or shelf technology have taken effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large grocery chains and retail tech vendors

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on, and the bill has not reached a vote where the split could be measured.

industries.industry: Large grocery chains (stores over 10,000 square feet)
industries.note: The bill caps their pricing with a gouging ban, bans them from using electronic shelf labels, and bars charging different shoppers different prices based on their data — directly limiting pricing tools these chains have been adopting. Their cost is the shopper's protection.

industries.industry: Electronic shelf label and retail display technology vendors
industries.note: Large grocery stores could not buy or use their core product at all under Section 5, removing their biggest retail market even for tags used to display a single honest price.

industries.industry: Facial recognition and in-store surveillance analytics vendors
industries.note: The bill bans surveillance-based price setting using facial recognition and requires stores to disclose any facial-recognition use at the entrance, shrinking the market for in-store biometric monitoring.

industries.industry: Smaller grocers (stores 10,000 square feet or smaller)
industries.note: The electronic shelf label ban exempts stores 10,000 square feet or smaller, so small grocers could keep digital tags their larger competitors must remove — a relative competitive edge, though the gouging and surveillance-pricing bans apply to them too.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that arrive in committee with single-party sponsorship and no committee action in their first months rarely reach the floor; this one would most plausibly advance only if attached to a larger consumer-protection or Farm Bill package, or if grocery pricing becomes a live political issue in the 2026 campaign. Without Republican cosponsors, a stand-alone Senate floor vote is unlikely this session.
